figures.caption: Fig. 1. Framework for transfer learning-based TMP prediction in MBRs: (a) treatment process of the target plant, and the associated prediction challenges: limited data, missing data and noisy measurements, (b) key characteristics of the three source plants: larger dataset size, higher data quality, and similar process config­ urations, (c) pretraining workflow of the LSTM and XGBoost models using data from the three source plants, (d) workflow for fine-tuning the base models using the target plant dataset to obtain the transfer learning models, (e) model interpretability and statistical analysis using LOFO and SHAP analyses.

Fig. 2. Operational context of the target MBR plant and source–target dataset characteristics: (a) TMP profile of the target plant during the monitoring period, (b) photograph of the MBR module at the target plant, (c) distributions of the operational and physicochemical variables in the three source plants and the target plant, (d) mean values of these variables for each plant.

Fig. 3. Source–target data distribution, feature collinearity, and predictive performance of the base models: (a) joint PCA of the source and target plant datasets, (b) feature–feature (X–X) Pearson correlation heatmap, and prediction scatter plots for (c) XGBoost-base and (d) LSTM-base.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Physicochemical evidence supporting the EPS- and SMP-related attribution pattern learned by LSTM-base in the source plants: EEM spectra of EPS from (a) Plant 1, (b) Plant 2, and (c) Plant 3; (d) sludge particle-size distributions of Plants 1–3 and the target plant; LC-OCD-derived organic fraction concentrations in (e) SMP and (f) effluent from Plants 1–3.

Fig. 5. Effect of fine-tuning ratio on target plant prediction performance and LOFO analysis: (a) R2, (b) RMSE, and (c) MAE as functions of fine-tuning ratio, (d) observed versus predicted TMP values for the baseline model, XGBoost-FT, and LSTM-FT on the target plant testing set, with the transfer models evaluated at FT = 40%, and (e) LOFO analysis results for LSTM-FT at FT = 40%. For each nonzero FT setting in (a)–(c), performance is reported as mean ± standard deviation across all fine-tuning segments and repeated runs, using up to six contiguous segments sampled from the fine-tuning pool and five random seeds for each retained segment.

Fig. 6. SHAP attribution patterns and LLM-assisted summary for LSTM-base and LSTM-FT: SHAP summary plots of (a) LSTM-base, (b) LSTM-FT at FT = 0, (c) LSTM- FT at FT = 40%, (d) LLM-assisted summary of the corresponding SHAP observations.

Fig. 7. Physicochemical evidence supporting the EPS-centered attribution pattern learned by LSTM-FT in the target plant: Mixed-liquor properties, including (a) CST and specific CST and (d) viscosity and specific viscosity; EEM spectra of (b) EPS and (c) SMP; (e) total iron concentrations in cleaning solutions collected during the two-step clean-in-place (CIP) procedure, and (f) TOC concentrations in cleaning solutions collected during sodium hypochlorite cleaning. Before CIP, the membrane unit was drained and rinsed with filtrate. The two-step CIP consisted of citric-acid cleaning (15 g/L, pH = 2.5) followed by sodium hypochlorite cleaning (1 g/L, pH = 10), with samples collected immediately before and after each cleaning step. B-CA and A-CA denote samples collected before and after citric-acid cleaning, respectively, whereas B-NaClO and A-NaClO denote samples collected before and after sodium hypochlorite cleaning.

figures.caption: Fig. 8. Additional validation of the proposed transfer learning framework in an industrial wastewater MBR: (a) TMP profile with major operational events, (b) summary statistics of the operational and physicochemical variables in the industrial MBR, (c) the pretrained LSTM model before and after fine-tuning, evaluated at FT = 0 and FT = 40% using R2, MAE, and RMSE, and (d) mean absolute SHAP values of LSTM-FT at FT = 40%.
